coredata.dc:description: Groundwater contamination by 1,2-dichloroethane (1,2-DCA) poses significant environmental and health risks. However, conventional in situ chemical oxidation (ISCO) methods are constrained by inefficient mass transfer, leading to suboptimal remediation outcomes. This study developed a pump-and-treat enhanced in situ chemical oxidation (ISCO-P) system employing sodium persulphate (activated by sodium hydroxide). Considering the two-phase partitioning characteristics of 1,2-DCA, we proposed a rapid estimation method for remediation agent dosage grounded in the Freundlich isotherm model. Laboratory-scale simulations demonstrated that hydrodynamic regulation optimizes density-driven contaminant transport dynamics in heterogeneous aquifers. This enhancement coupling reduced the remediation duration from molecular diffusion-dominated processes (traditional ISCO) to 6 days, while expanding effective treatment zones by eightfold. Field applications confirmed the efficacy of the technology: optimised well configurations achieved 20–30 m remediation agent diffusion radii, with 95.7 % reduction in 1,2-DCA concentration within 7 months and sustained stabilisation below 147 μg/L. Byproduct risks (e.g., sulphate levels and pH fluctuations) remained controlled for over 31-month operational period. By resolving the key engineering challenges in ISCO implementation-specifically agent quantification and mass transfer efficiency-this work provides a strategic framework for sustainable organic groundwater remediation.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Groundwater contamination by 1,2-dichloroethane (1,2-DCA) poses significant environmental and health risks. However, conventional in situ chemical oxidation (ISCO) methods are constrained by inefficient mass transfer, leading to suboptimal remediation outcomes. This study developed a pump-and-treat enhanced in situ chemical oxidation (ISCO-P) system employing sodium persulphate (activated by sodium hydroxide). Considering the two-phase partitioning characteristics of 1,2-DCA, we proposed a rapid estimation method for remediation agent dosage grounded in the Freundlich isotherm model. Laboratory-scale simulations demonstrated that hydrodynamic regulation optimizes density-driven contaminant transport dynamics in heterogeneous aquifers. This enhancement coupling reduced the remediation duration from molecular diffusion-dominated processes (traditional ISCO) to 6 days, while expanding effective treatment zones by eightfold. Field applications confirmed the efficacy of the technology: optimised well configurations achieved 20–30 m remediation agent diffusion radii, with 95.7 % reduction in 1,2-DCA concentration within 7 months and sustained stabilisation below 147 μg/L. Byproduct risks (e.g., sulphate levels and pH fluctuations) remained controlled for over 31-month operational period. By resolving the key engineering challenges in ISCO implementation-specifically agent quantification and mass transfer efficiency-this work provides a strategic framework for sustainable organic groundwater remediation.

ce:section.ce:para: 1,2-dichloroethane (1,2-DCA), a critical intermediate in polyvinyl chloride production and an industrial solvent, has been listed as a priority pollutant in environmental priority substance lists of multiple European and American countries due to its high toxicity (carcinogenicity and hepatorenal toxicity risks) [1]. This chlorinated hydrocarbon exhibits distinct physicochemical characteristics: high density (1.25 g/cm3, 20 °C), low aqueous solubility (8.7 g/L, 20 °C), limited mobility, and resistance to degradation. These properties facilitate its penetration through the vadose zone and subsequent persistence in subsurface porous media, establishing long-term contamination sources in subsurface environments [2].

For chlorinated dense non-aqueous phase liquids such as 1,2-DCA, in situ chemical oxidation (ISCO) represents one of the most effective remediation technologies [3]. This approach involves injecting oxidants (e.g., potassium permanganate and sodium persulphate) into contaminated aquifers to degrade 1,2-DCA into less toxic or benign substances (e.g., chloride ions, carbon dioxide, and water), offering advantages such as rapid remediation kinetics and low secondary contamination risks. However, field-scale ISCO applications face two critical operational constraints. (1) Remediation agent demand underestimation, wherein traditional ISCO designs rely on dissolved-phase contaminant concentrations to estimate remediation agent demand, neglecting the sorbed contaminants retained by aquifer media. This oversight substantially underestimates actual reagent requirements, resulting in contaminant concentration rebound due to depletion of the remediation agent [4]. (2) Spatial limitations in remediation agent delivery, wherein the effective radius of remediation agent influence is constrained by heterogeneous media permeability, with preferential transport through high-permeability zones and limited diffusion into low-permeability regions [5]. Field observations indicate typical diffusion radii of 1.5–3 m, necessitating dense injection well arrays (spacing <5 m) to achieve remediation targets [6]. This configuration substantially increases both construction costs and long-term monitoring complexity. Consequently, recent advancements have explored mitigation strategies including nanomaterial-enhanced remediation agent delivery [7], surfactant-mediated solubilisation [8], and microbially-mediated chemical oxidation [9]. However, although these innovations partially alleviate mass transfer limitations, they fail to fundamentally overcome the inherent constraints of passive diffusion-dominated transport mechanisms in low-permeability zones, leaving the challenge of compromised remediation efficiency unresolved.

Therefore, this study proposes an ISCO-P technology, which transforms the remediation agent transport from passive diffusion to hydrodynamic advection diffusion by regulating hydraulic gradients through groundwater extraction and reinjection [10]. A sodium hydroxide (NaOH)-activated persulphate (Na2S2O8) oxidation system was employed, activating both radical (SO4 −· and ·OH) and nonradical (1O2) degradation pathways [11]. A rapid estimation method for total remediation agent dosage based on the two-phase partitioning characteristics of 1,2-DCA is proposed. Laboratory-scale model simulations were conducted to analyse 1,2-DCA contaminant plume formation and compare the enhancement mechanisms of hydrodynamic control between ISCO and ISCO-P technologies. Further numerical simulations and field implementation validations of ISCO-P demonstrated its applicability in practical remediation scenarios. This approach provides an efficient, cost-effective, and sustainable solution for engineered remediation of chlorinated hydrocarbon-contaminated sites.

This study investigated an organically contaminated site at a decommissioned chemical plant. The stratigraphic sequence comprised four distinct layers (Fig. 1a): plain fill (anthropogenic deposits), silty clay (low-permeability cohesive soil), gravel (coarse-grained aquifer medium), and mudstone (impermeable bedrock). The aquifer system, primarily hosted within a gravel phreatic aquifer at depths of 15.00–29.00 m, exhibited a natural groundwater flow direction from south to north with a 0.36 % hydraulic gradient. This aquifer demonstrated a hydraulic conductivity range of 2.98–21.02 m/d and a specific yield of 1.01–1.15 L/(s·m).

Historical contamination stems from point-source contamination caused by improper disposal of chlorinated organic solvents and solid wastes. The contamination plume was categorised into three distinct zones based on the 1,2-DCA concentrations as: the plume fringe zone (0–1000 μg/L), the plume core zone (1000–2000 μg/L), and the source zone (2000–6000 μg/L) (Fig. 1b).

The experimental gravel samples were collected from the aquifer stratum at the study site, exhibiting particle shapes dominated by subrounded forms with minor occurrences of well-rounded and subangular grains. The primary lithological composition consisted of moderately weathered quartz and siliceous rocks. The particle size distribution ranged from 0.075 to 200 mm, with the majority predominantly distributed within 0.25–60.00 mm. Major variations in surface microtextures were observed across different particle sizes. Representative gravels with diameters (D) of 0.25, 0.50, and 2.00 cm were selected for scanning electron microscopy analysis (Fig. 2 ). The microstructural parameters are systematically documented in Table S1.
All chemicals, including 1,2-dichloroethane (1,2-DCA; 1000 μg/mL in methanol), sodium hydroxide (NaOH; ≥96.0 %), and sodium persulphate (Na2S2O8; ≥98.0 %); were used as received.

Screened gravel samples with D = 0.25, 0.50, and 2.00 cm were oven-dried at 105 °C until constant weight, followed by cooling and airtight storage. The adsorption-desorption experiments were conducted using the following procedures: Gravel samples (25.0 ± 3.0 g, exact mass recorded) were placed in 100 mL amber glass bottles in triplicate (n = 3). A 50 mL solution of 1,2-DCA with concentration gradients of 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, and 5000 μg/L was added to each bottle. The mixtures were manually shaken for 30 s and equilibrated at 25.0 ± 0.5 °C (reflecting the annual mean temperature of the study region). Sampling (1 mL per aliquot) occurred at 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 12 h to measure residual 1,2-DCA concentrations. After 24 h of equilibrium adsorption, the residual liquid was removed, and 50 mL of ultrapure water was introduced to initiate desorption. ce:section.ce:section-title: Laboratory-scale simulation of the ISCO and ISCO-P technologies for plume remediation
ce:section.ce:para: The experimental setup for simulating the 1,2-DCA contaminant plume in a single-well remediation system utilised a polyethene sandbox (1.0 m × 1.0 m × 0.7 m) filled with sieved gravel (particle size ≤ 0.25 cm) to a thickness of 0.6 m (Fig. 3 ). Thirty-two monitoring wells (J1–1 to J8–4) and one reagent injection well (ZYJ) were constructed using PVC pipes with sealed caps. The entire system was enclosed with transparent plastic film to ensure airtight conditions. The three-phase experimental protocol sequentially investigated plume formation and remediation efficacy between the ISCO and ISCO-P technologies.

Phase 1 established the contaminant plume through the subsurface injection of 0.18 g of 1,2-DCA through ZYJ. Concentration stabilisation (defined as<5 % variation across three consecutive monitoring durations) was verified through systematic 20-day interval sampling across all monitoring wells.

Phase 2 implemented ISCO remediation through sequential ZYJ injections of 0.33 L of 30 % (w/w) NaOH solution followed by 1 L of 300 g/L Na₂S₂O₈ solution. Plume evolution was tracked by systematically sampling all monitoring points at 7-day intervals to assess remediation agent delivery and contaminant degradation kinetics. Sampling depths (h) were configured at 10, 30, and 50 cm, with radial distances (R) from the ZYJ injection point defined as follows: R = 0 cm at ZYJ, R = 10 cm for monitoring wells J1–1 to J8–1, R = 20 cm for J1–2 to J8–2, and R = 30 cm for J1–3 to J8–3.

Phase 3 evaluated ISCO-P enhancement by repeating Phase 2 protocols after system flushing (until effluent 1,2-DCA concentrations fell below detection limits) and plume re-establishment. A pumping circulation system was activated to enhance reagent distribution, with contaminant transport dynamics monitored through high-frequency sampling at 2-day intervals.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Numerical 1,2-DCA contamination remediation modeling using ISCO-P technology
ce:section.ce:para: A numerical simulation model was established for the experimental site to simulate the ISCO-P remediation process of 1,2-DCA contamination. The groundwater conceptual model was constructed using the MODFLOW module [14] in GMS 7.0, while the MT3DMS module was employed to simulate the transport of remediation agents [15]. The remediation area (approximately 120,000 m2) was discretised into unstructured meshes (Triangular Prism grid type). The well configuration comprised 198 chemical injection wells arranged with 30-m spacing in the north-south direction, and 20-m spacing in the east-west direction (Fig. 4 ). The simulation scenarios were configured in two sequential phases: (1) Hydrodynamic control employed pumping wells operating at 150 m3/d per well to establish hydraulic gradients controlling groundwater flow directions and creating capture zones to prevent off-site contaminant migration. (2) Chemical remediation introduced liquid alkali (30 % w/w sodium hydroxide) and sodium persulphate solution (300 kg/ m3) through injection wells at 50 m3/d per well. The transport behaviour of these remediation agents was monitored under the simulated coupled advection-dispersion processes.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Field implementation of 1,2-DCA contaminated site remediation with ISCO-P technology
ce:section.ce:para: The experiment was divided into three phases: preparation, implementation, and monitoring.

(1) Preparation Phase: Extraction wells (Fig. 5a) were activated for hydrodynamic regulation, with extracted groundwater reinjected into injection wells to control the hydraulic gradient within the contaminated zone. The extraction and injection well layout is shown in Fig. 4a.

(2) Implementation Phase (remediation agent injection phase): Industrial-grade sodium persulphate (Na₂S₂O₈, 99 % purity) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 30 % liquid solution) were used as the oxidant and activator, respectively. Sodium persulphate was injected at a concentration of 300 kg/m3, with injection well locations consistent with Fig. 4b and injection stations shown in Fig. 5b. Each injection well received a cumulative dosage of 1.5 tons of Na₂S₂O₈ and 0.7 m3 of NaOH. Post-injection, continuous extraction and reinjection were maintained until groundwater 1,2-DCA concentrations fell below the remediation target of 147 μg/L, after which hydrodynamic control ceased. The remediation target (147 μg/L) was derived from the site-specific risk assessment, aligning with China's screening level for 1,2-DCA in groundwater.

(3) Monitoring Phase: A network of 13 monitoring wells (Fig. 5c) was established, comprising three wells in the source zone, three in the plume zone, and seven along the plume boundary. Groundwater samples were collected using a portable bladder pump (QED MP50, QED Environmental Systems, USA) with low-flow purging. Field measurements of pH were conducted using a HACH Q300HD portable water quality analyser (HACH, USA). Sulphate concentrations were analysed via ion chromatography, while 1,2-DCA levels were quantified using purge and trap gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) with an Agilent 7890 gas chromatograph equipped with an electron capture detector (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), with a limit of detection of 0.05 μg/L. Sampling was performed monthly over 31 months.

ce:section.ce:para:
The equilibrium adsorption-desorption capacity versus initial concentration curves for gravel is shown in Fig. S1. As the initial concentration
C e
increased, the adsorption capacity
q t
of gravel for 1,2-DCA gradually rose to saturation. Gravel with diameters D = 0.25, 0.50, and 2.00 cm exhibited saturated adsorption capacities of 1.42, 1.49, and 1.83 μg/g, respectively, indicating substantially enhanced adsorption with larger particle sizes. Specifically, the D = 2.00 cm gravel possessed the largest average pore diameter of 12.88 nm (Table S1), which facilitated greater pore channel volume for macromolecule accommodation and reduced steric hindrance effects [19]. Moreover, this phenomenon correlates strongly with the heterogeneous surface structures of gravel: Gravel (D = 0.25 cm) displayed limited adsorption sites due to smooth surfaces with scattered debris and indistinct pores (Fig. 2). Gravel (D = 2.00 cm) exhibited rough surfaces with uniformly distributed irregular ridges, providing higher specific surface area and enhanced adsorption site density [20]. Gravel (D = 0.50 cm) showed flat, dense structures with minimal surface features, resulting in the lowest adsorption capacity. Further, the desorption quantities of gravel ranged from 0.06 to 0.61 μg/g (desorption rate: 9.51–42.81 %), with larger gravel (D = 2.00 cm) demonstrating lower desorption capacity and higher residual adsorption compared to smaller counterparts, attributed to stronger adsorption-site interactions in textured surfaces.

The adsorption-desorption capacity for gravel was analysed using the Langmuir, Freundlich, Temkin, and D-R models (Figs. S2 and S3). The Freundlich model demonstrated excellent fitting performance with determination coefficients (R2) exceeding 0.99 (Table S2), indicating a strong correlation between the adsorption capacity (
q t
) of 1,2-DCA and its equilibrium liquid-phase (
C e
) concentration as described by the Freundlich equation. The linear exponent in the adsorption phase, though slightly above 1, suggests a nonlinear multilayer adsorption mechanism on gravel surfaces with moderate heterogeneity. This behaviour aligns with the characteristic Freundlich adsorption pattern on heterogeneous surfaces [21]. The Freundlich constant (K
f ), which quantifies the binding affinity between adsorbate and adsorbent [22], exhibited distinct values during adsorption (0.59) and desorption (0.06–0.08) phases (Table S2). This disparity indicates a stronger adsorption capacity of 1,2-DCA on gravels compared to its desorption potential, demonstrating a pronounced adsorption-desorption hysteresis effect. Such hysteresis aligns with field observations of persistent 1,2-DCA retention in aquifers [23]. Notably, the narrow variation range of the K
f values across gravels with differing particle sizes (0.59 ± 0.03 during adsorption; 0.07 ± 0.01 during desorption) suggests minimal particle size influence on adsorption capacity. This implies that the adsorption process is predominantly governed by surface chemical properties, particularly the coordination of carbonate groups [8], rather than variations in physical structural parameters like specific surface area or pore distribution.

In summary, the novel methodology proposed in this study estimates the medium-adsorbed inventory based on aqueous-phase dissolved concentration and subsequently determines the total mass of 1,2-DCA in the aquifer system. This approach revises conventional calculation methods by enabling direct computation of the remediation agent dosage through readily measurable parameters (aqueous-phase dissolved concentration), thereby integrating practical applicability with scientific rigour.

ce:section.ce:section-title: 1,2-DCA diffusion simulation in the simulated aquifer
ce:section.ce:para: The transport behaviour of 1,2-DCA in a heterogeneous aquifer was investigated using a laboratory sandbox, which revealed density-driven transport characteristics (Fig. 6a). After 60 days of continuous dispersion, a relatively stable contaminant plume was formed. During the vertical transport phase (0–5 days), the upper-layer (h = 10 cm) concentration at the injection centre decreased, while the lower-layer (h = 30 cm) concentration increased, reaching equilibrium across all layers by day 5. At this stage, the maximum concentration (62,300 μg/L) was observed in the lower layer (h = 30 cm). Subsequently, during the horizontal transport phase (5–60 days), migration velocity decreased due to diminishing concentration gradients.

The distribution of 1,2-DCA concentrations at day 60 exhibited pronounced spatial heterogeneity (Fig. 6b). Vertical concentration gradients followed a downward-increasing pattern, where the lower-layer (h = 30 cm) concentrations exceeded those in the middle layer (h = 20 cm) by 7.70–14.10 %, while the middle layer (h = 20 cm) showed 15.5–38.9 % higher concentrations than the upper layer (h = 10 cm). This stratification originated from the density contrast of the 1,2-DCA (relative water density of 1.235), which promoted gravitational settling to the aquifer base, forming persistent contamination sources retained in porous media. The centre of the plume (R = 0 cm) maintained elevated concentrations ranging from 2421 to 3102 μg/L. At radial distances of 10, 20, and 30 cm from the centre, average 1,2-DCA concentrations decreased by 68.8 %, 12.4 %, and 7.0 %, respectively, relative to the central values. The observed concentration decay with increasing radial distance exhibited a decreasing rate of attenuation. This transport behaviour is attributed to the physicochemical characteristics of 1,2-DCA. Under gravitational forces, 1,2-DCA tends to become entrapped within the pores of the aquifer matrix [27]. Its limited hydrophobicity, as indicated by a low octanol-water partition coefficient (KOW = 1.48) [28], facilitates gradual migration with groundwater flow. These properties collectively lead to the formation of persistent, slow-moving point contamination sources in aquifers.
Remediation agents were injected at the plume centre in both ISCO and ISCO-P processes. The 1,2-DCA concentrations during remediation are illustrated in Fig. 7 .

For ISCO, the remediation duration lasted 28 days. Remediation agent injection reduced 1,2-DCA concentrations in the injection well (ZYJ) and the R = 10 cm monitoring well from 3000.35 μg/L and 1080.00 μg/L to 50.05 μg/L (98.33 % removal) and 202.15 μg/L (81.28 % removal), respectively. The effective remediation radius (>80 % removal) was limited to 10 cm, with efficiency declining exponentially with distance. In contrast, ISCO-P achieved remediation within 6 days. The 1,2-DCA concentrations decreased rapidly, accompanied by significant contraction of high-concentration zones. By day 7, hydraulic shearing fragmented the plume at R = 10 cm into an upper high-concentration sub-plume and a lower low-concentration sub-plume (Fig. 7). Continuous groundwater extraction and reinjection elevated removal efficiencies to 98.62, 98.11, and 98.54 % at R = 10, 20, and 30 cm, respectively.

Compared to ISCO, the ISCO-P process upgraded the mass transfer mechanism to advection-dominated transport [29,30], notably enhancing the convective-diffusive synergistic transport of remediation agents. Specifically, hydraulic shearing disrupted plume continuity (with plume fragmentation observed on day 7, as shown in Fig. 7), accelerating contaminant-remediation agent interfacial renewal, while forced convection reconstructed dynamic remediation agent concentration gradients to improve both mass transfer and reaction rates synchronously. These combined effects reduced the remediation duration to 6 days (4.7-fold acceleration compared to conventional ISCO) and expanded effective treatment zones by approximately eightfold. The results demonstrate that hydrodynamic control effectively overcomes medium heterogeneity and enhances multi-scale mass transfer efficiency [31]. Through coupled hydrodynamic-chemical interactions, this approach promotes reagent transport and expands remediation scope, confirming the application potential of active mass transfer control in heterogeneous site remediation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Validation of ISCO-P technology for remediation of 1,2-DCA contaminated site

ce:section.ce:para: The simulation results of the ISCO-P field application are shown in Fig. 8 . In this application simulation, the layout range of injection wells exceeded the remediation boundaries of 1,2-DCA, effectively preventing plume expansion and secondary contamination caused by injection activities. Under hydrodynamic control, the groundwater head in pumping well areas exhibited notable declines, forming a large cone of depression, while injection well areas developed high-head zones (Fig. 8a). The groundwater flow direction remained unchanged, but the hydraulic gradients increased substantially. Considering advection, dispersion, medium adsorption-desorption, and remediation agent-mediated pollutant degradation, the 28-day remediation agent diffusion range in groundwater is illustrated in Fig. 8b. In upstream injection well areas, the remediation agents radially diffused from wells under high-head conditions, achieving extensive migration. In downstream pumping well areas, the remediation agents formed high-concentration zones with pronounced migration trends along groundwater flow paths.

Compared to the traditional ISCO technology, the ISCO-P system optimised the remediation duration and substantially reduced economic costs. The hydrodynamic control well clusters established directional hydraulic circulation for the remediation duration, compressing the simulated remediation duration from 330 days (conventional ISCO) to 210 days by overcoming mass transfer inefficiencies. Economically, the conventional ISCO technique exhibited limited remediation agent diffusion radii (1.5–3 m), necessitating dense injection well networks. In contrast, the ISCO-P technology enhanced the remediation agent diffusion radius to 20–30 m by installing 36 hydrodynamic control well clusters, thereby eliminating the need for hundreds of injection wells and achieving multimillion RMB cost savings in infrastructure and operational expenditures. Furthermore, the ISCO-P-directed mass transfer mechanism minimised non-target reactions (e.g., competitive consumption by reduced metals) that often increase treatment costs in conventional ISCO [32,33]. By enhancing persulphate diffusion efficiency through hydrodynamic optimisation, ISCO-P eliminated redundant well clusters caused by low-efficiency mass transfer while improving reagent utilisation through precise flow field control, achieving the synergistic optimisation of remediation efficiency and cost-effectiveness.
Field remediation and monitoring over 31 months revealed changes in average 1,2-DCA concentrations, sulphate levels, and pH (Fig. 9 ).

The 1,2-DCA concentrations met remediation targets by the 7th month, with 74.7 %, 91.3 %, and 95.7 % reductions in the plume fringe zone, plume core zone, and source zones, respectively. Concentrations remained stable below targets during the subsequent 24-month monitoring. During ISCO-P implementation, remediation agents spread throughout the remediation zone via advection and dispersion, corroborating the accuracy of remediation agent diffusion simulations.

The high-volume injection of remediation agents triggered marked fluctuations in sulphate concentrations and pH levels during the initial remediation phase. Specifically, the source zone, plume core zone, and plume fringe zone exhibited peak pH values of 10.9, 10.6, and 9.1, respectively, within the first 15 days of treatment. Concurrently, sulphate concentrations in these zones reached maximum values of 413,890, 435,461, and 417,400 μg/L, respectively, after 1.5 months of remediation initiation. Both parameters gradually decreased to baseline levels and stabilised throughout the subsequent monitoring period. Long-term monitoring over 31 months revealed that groundwater sulphate concentrations consistently remained below 350 μg/L, thereby meeting the Class IV water quality criteria specified in the Chinese standard for groundwater quality (GB/T 14848–2017). This compliance confirmed the absence of byproduct risks associated with the remediation process. The persulphate-activated ISCO technology exhibited high remediation efficiency for targeted groundwater contaminants. Notably, the sodium persulphate (activated by sodium hydroxide) system employed in this study demonstrated environmental compatibility. The transient nature of pH and sulphate perturbations, coupled with their rapid return to environmental background values, underscores the system's operational stability and suitability for field-scale applications in heterogeneous aquifer environments.

This study developed an enhanced ISCO process incorporating hydrodynamic manipulation through pumping-reinjection well arrays to address the intrinsic mass transfer limitations encountered in conventional ISCO applications for heterogeneous aquifer remediation scenarios. The principal outcomes are detailed as follows:
(1)
The adsorption of 1,2-DCA on aquifer gravels follows a nonlinear multilayer mechanism. Surface chemical properties rather than particle size distribution governed adsorption capacity variation, with Freundlich isotherm linearization enabling accurate quantification of total contaminant mass from aqueous phase concentrations. This mathematical approach established critical parameters for oxidant dosage determination in ISCO-P applications.
(2)
Density-driven migration characteristics of 1,2-DCA in heterogeneous aquifers demonstrated distinct temporal phases: vertical dispersion dominance during initial 0–5 days followed by horizontal propagation controlled by concentration gradients over the subsequent 5–60-day period. Stratification analysis revealed 7.70–14.10 % higher contaminant accumulation in lower aquifer zones (h = 30 cm) compared to intermediate layers (h = 20 cm), with adsorption-desorption hysteresis and hydraulic conductivity jointly governing spatial attenuation patterns.
(3)
Comparative remediation simulations by sandbox tests confirmed the advantages of ISCO-P over conventional ISCO. The enhanced process achieved eightfold expansion of oxidant dispersion radius (80 cm vs 10 cm) and shortened remediation duration from 28 days to 6 days through accelerated agent transportation. These results confirm that hydrodynamic control addresses multi-scale mass transfer limitations in heterogeneous media.
(4)
Field implementation verified the technical framework, with directional flow fields from optimised well clusters extending oxidant influence radii to 20–30 m. Numerical modeling predicted 36 % reduction in remediation duration and proportional cost savings. Operational data confirmed 95.7 % 1,2-DCA concentration reduction within 7 months, achieving sustained compliance with regulatory thresholds (147 μg/L). Secondary parameters including pH (4.9–5.1) and sulphate levels (42.02–48.19 mg/L) remained within background ranges throughout the 24-month monitoring period, demonstrating effective process control.
